1G (Number Theory)

Words: 247 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 247
1G OurBigBook.com
An Euler pseudoprime is an odd composite number N with gcd(b,N)=1 satisfying b(N−1)/2≡(Nb​)(modN), where the right side is the Jacobi symbol. A weaker convention requires only b(N−1)/2≡±1; it is distinguished below. A strong pseudoprime, with N−1=2sd and d odd, satisfies bd≡1 or b2jd≡−1 for some 0≤j<s.
By the Chinese remainder theorem for unit groups, the unit group modulo 65 is C4​×C12​. Modulo 5, b32=1. Thus the only possible sign in b32≡±1(mod65) is positive. Modulo 13, writing b=ge for a primitive root, the condition is 12∣32e, equivalently 3∣e. Consequently b has multiplicative order dividing 4 in each factor. Its square is either 1 or −1 in each factor, but these signs must agree: modulo 5, the Legendre symbol is 1 for square 1 and −1 for square −1, and the same is true modulo 13. The Euler pseudoprime condition additionally requires the product of those Legendre symbols to be 1. Hence
65 is an Euler pseudoprime to b⟺b2≡±1(mod65).​
(1)
Each sign has two roots modulo each prime, hence four roots modulo 65. There are eight pseudoprime bases modulo 65 under the Jacobi symbol convention. Under the weaker sign-only convention there are instead sixteen pseudoprime bases, since the two signs of the squares need not agree; the stated equivalence therefore specifically uses the Jacobi symbol convention.
For the strong pseudoprime condition, s=6,d=1. Since the unit group has exponent of a finite group 12, the only possibilities are b=±1 or b2=−1. The six pseudoprime bases are 1,8,18,47,57,64. For example 82=182≡−1, while 8⋅18≡14 has 142≡1 but 14≡±1. Thus the strong-pseudoprime pseudoprime bases are not a subgroup.

3G (Coding & Cryptography)

Words: 176 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 176
3G OurBigBook.com
Identify a binary word with its coefficient polynomial in R=F2​[X]/(X7−1). A cyclic code is exactly an ideal of R: closure under multiplication by X is closure under cyclic shift. Its inverse image in the principal ideal domain F2​[X] has a unique monic generator polynomial of a cyclic code g dividing X7−1. Put
a=X+1,b=X3+X+1,c=X3+X2+1;X7−1=abc.
(4)
The cubics have no root in F2​, hence are irreducible polynomials. The eight monic divisors yield all binary cyclic codes of length seven. A code generated by g has basis g,Xg,…,X6−deggg and dimension 7−degg, with the zero code treated separately.
For the dual of a cyclic code, let h=(X7−1)/g. Orthogonality of coefficient vectors to all cyclic shifts gives the generator h∗(X)=Xdeghh(X−1). Here a∗=a,b∗=c,c∗=b. Thus the complete pairing, with the respective dimensions, is
1 (7)⟷abc (0),a (6)⟷bc (1),b (4)⟷ab (3),c (4)⟷ac (3).​
(5)
These are respectively the whole-space/zero, even-weight/repetition, and two Hamming code/binary simplex code pairs. The reciprocal formula follows because the product of a word polynomial and the reversed polynomial of an orthogonal word has zero coefficients in all cyclic positions; the resulting inclusion has the correct complementary dimension, hence is equality.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
In strict Chomsky normal form, every production of a context-free grammar is A→BC or A→a, with A,B,C nonterminal symbols and a a terminal symbol. Such a derivation cannot produce the empty word: it starts with one nonterminal symbol, and every step either increases the symbol count or replaces one symbol by one symbol. The context-free language {ε}, generated by S→ε, is therefore not generated by any strict CNF grammar.
The convention matters: extended Chomsky normal form permits S→ε with S excluded from right-hand sides. Under that convention every context-free language has such a grammar, so the requested example would not exist.

b

Words: 103 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 103
b OurBigBook.com
The context-free languages L1​={anbncm:n,m≥0} and L2​={ambncn:n,m≥0} have context-free grammars S→TC, T→aTb∣ε, C→cC∣ε, and S→AT, A→aA∣ε, T→bTc∣ε, respectively.
Their intersection is L={anbncn:n≥0}. Suppose L satisfied the pumping lemma for context-free languages with length p. In a decomposition apbpcp=uvwxy with ∣vwx∣≤p and ∣vx∣>0, the window vwx cannot meet both the a and c blocks. Pumping down changes at least one count and leaves at least one count unchanged. Thus the three counts are unequal, or the word order is invalid, contrary to the pumping lemma for context-free languages. Hence CFLs are not closed under intersection.

c

Words: 161 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 161
c OurBigBook.com
Context-free languages are closed under union: use a new start symbol with alternatives for two renamed context-free grammars. If they were closed under complement in Σ∗, De Morgan's laws would give
L1​∩L2​=Σ∗∖((Σ∗∖L1​)∪(Σ∗∖L2​)),
(6)
contradicting the preceding intersection example. Therefore some CFL has a non-context-free complement. This is an existence argument; it does not assert that both complements of the particular L1​,L2​ are non-context-free.
A concrete choice is L={a,b,c}∗∖{anbncn:n≥0}. Words outside a∗b∗c∗ form a regular language. Among words inside it, membership in L means the first two counts or the last two counts differ. Each unequal-count comparison has a context-free grammar: for aibj with i>j, use T→aTb∣A, A→aA∣a; for i<j, replace A by B→bB∣b. Append any number of c's, or prefix any number of a's for the analogous b,c comparison. Taking these unions gives a context-free language whose complement is the non-context-free equal-three-count language. These productions are definitions of the example, not a restriction to strict Chomsky normal form.

Write ℓ(β) for the log-likelihood and U=∇ℓ for the score function. Newton method uses the Observed Fisher information M=−∇2ℓ; Fisher scoring uses the Fisher information M=Eβ​[−∇2ℓ].
For independent responses in an exponential family, with fixed dispersion parameter and fixed weights ai​, a canonical link function gives θi​=xiT​β and
ℓ(β)=∑i​ai​yi​θi​−b(θi​)​+∑i​ci​(yi​),U=∑i​ai​xi​(yi​−b′(θi​))​,−∇2ℓ=∑i​ai​b′′(θi​)​xi​xiT​.
(7)
The last matrix depends on β but not on the responses, so taking its expectation leaves it unchanged. Hence the two updates are identical, wherever this Fisher information matrix is invertible. Equivalently both solve the same iteratively reweighted least squares problem. This statement concerns the regression coefficients at a fixed dispersion parameter; a joint update of an unknown dispersion parameter need not have identical observed and expected full Fisher information matrices.

6B (Mathematical Biology)

Solution

Words: 127
6B OurBigBook.com
In the birth-death master equation, The upward jump has rate λ and the downward jump rate βx, so the first two jump moments per unit time are A(x)=λ−βx and B(x)=λ+βx. The second-order Kramers-Moyal expansion gives the diffusion approximation of a birth-death process
∂t​P=−∂x​[(λ−βx)P]+21​∂x2​[(λ+βx)P].​
(8)
For the associated Fokker-Planck equation, integrating by parts with vanishing moment boundary terms gives d⟨f⟩/dt=⟨Af′+21​Bf′′⟩. Taking f=x,x2 yields
dtd⟨x⟩​=λ−β⟨x⟩,dtd⟨x2⟩​=−2β⟨x2⟩+(2λ+β)⟨x⟩+λ.​
(9)
For example, if m0​=⟨x(0)⟩, then m(t)=λ/β+(m0​−λ/β)e−βt, while the variance satisfies v′=−2βv+λ+βm. The two boxed moment equations also follow exactly from the discrete Markov jump-process generator, since quadratic functions have no higher jump terms. A reflecting diffusion confined to x≥0 can have extra boundary contributions; the formal approximation near extinction is not an exact replacement for the discrete process.

7E (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 128 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 128
7E OurBigBook.com
After division by z, the coefficients are P=2/z−1 and Q=−1/z. At 0, zP and z2Q are analytic functions, so 0 is a regular singular point. Its indicial equation is r(r−1)+2r=r(r+1)=0. There are no other finite singular points of a differential equation. At infinity the regular singular point criterion for a second-order equation would require P=O(z−1), but P→−1; hence infinity is an irregular singular point.
Substituting y=f/z reduces the equation to f′′−f′=0, so
y(z)=zA+Bez​,z=0.​
(10)
A linearly independent pair is 1/z and (ez−1)/z. Their Wronskian is ez/z2=0. The second has a removable singularity at 0 and value 1, whereas the first has a simple pole, agreeing with the two characteristic exponents at a regular singular point, 0,−1. The integer difference does not require a logarithm. At infinity ez/z has an essential singularity, consistent with the irregular singular point; the existence of the simpler solution 1/z does not make infinity regular.

Liouville integrability on a 2n-dimensional symplectic manifold means that there are n functionally independent first integrals, including H, whose pairwise Poisson brackets vanish. Near a compact connected regular common level set, the Arnold-Liouville theorem gives action-angle variables (Ji​,θi​) with Ji​=(2π)−1∮pdq, θi​ periodic modulo 2π, H=H(J), J˙i​=0 and θ˙i​=∂H/∂Ji​.
For a frozen mass, the turning point is q∗​=(2E)1/(2k). The action variable is
J=π2​∫0q∗​​2m(E−q2k/2)​dq=Ck​m1/2E(k+1)/(2k),Ck​=π22​21/(2k)​∫01​1−s2k​ds.
(11)
Adiabatic invariance of the action holds to leading order when the mass varies slowly compared with an orbital period, away from degenerating orbits. Keeping J fixed gives
E(t)∝m(t)−k/(k+1),c=−k+1k​.​
(12)
For k=1 this agrees with E=ωJ and ω∝m−1/2.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Chemical equilibrium imposes μe​+μp​=μH​+μγ​. For blackbody photons, μγ​=0. Define the positive Hydrogen binding energy by I=(me​+mp​−mH​)c2, approximately 13.6eV. Multiplying the two Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution number densities and dividing by the neutral-hydrogen density gives
nH​ne​np​​=gH​ge​gp​​(h22πkT​mH​me​mp​​)3/2e−I/(kT).
(13)
Use ge​gp​/gH​=1 and mp​/mH​≃1 to obtain the Saha ionization equation
nH​ne​np​​=(h22πme​kT​)3/2e−I/(kT).​
(14)
The assumptions are nonrelativistic, dilute, nondegenerate species at a common temperature, ground-state hydrogen with the stated degeneracy factors, negligible mass correction in the prefactor, and sufficiently rapid reactions to maintain chemical equilibrium.

b

Words: 83 Articles: 1
9C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 83
b OurBigBook.com
The baryon-to-photon ratio is extremely small, of order 10−9. Thus even when the typical photon energy is below I, the high-energy tail of the blackbody radiation contains enough photons above the ionization energy to reionize almost every newly formed hydrogen atom. Cosmological recombination becomes effective only when this exponentially small tail is also small compared with the baryon-to-photon ratio. Consequently recombination occurs at a temperature much lower than I/k, consistent with kT≃0.03I. The exact freeze-out history also depends on reaction rates and expansion; the equilibrium estimate explains the large suppression of the temperature.

T(a)=(a1​10​),M=T(a1​)⋯T(am​),B=T(a0​),N=BMB−1.

Periodicity says that M fixes θ1​ as a Möbius transformation, while B takes θ1​ to d​. Thus N=(AC​B1​D​) has integer entries and fixes d​. Equating rational and irrational parts in Ad​+B1​=d​(Cd​+D) gives A=D,B1​=dC. Consequently
A2−dC2=detN=(−1)m.

a OurBigBook.com
A many-one reduction A≤m​B is a total computable function f:N→N with x∈A⟺f(x)∈B. If B is recursively enumerable, compute f(x) and run a semidecision procedure for B on that value. It halts exactly when x∈A, so A is recursively enumerable. Totality of f is essential to this argument.

Words: 97 Articles: 1
11H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 97
b OurBigBook.com
The S-m-n theorem says that parameters can be compiled effectively into program indices: for a standard effective numbering, there is a total computable function smn​ with φsmn​(e,a)​(x)=φe​(a,x) for partial computable functions of m+n arguments.
Write K={e:φe​(e) halts}, a recursively enumerable halting problem. If X is recursively enumerable, make a program with parameter x which ignores its input and runs a semidecision procedure for x∈X, halting when that procedure halts. By the S-m-n theorem its index f(x) is total computable and f(x)∈K⟺x∈X. Conversely, X≤m​K implies that X is recursively enumerable by the previous construction. Thus X is r.e.⟺X≤m​K​.

Use uniform finite-stage enumerations Wn,s​ and Ks​. Define a uniformly recursively enumerable set
Vn​={x:∃s (x∈Ks​ and x<∣Wn,s​∣)}.
(21)
The S-m-n theorem supplies a total computable index function f with Wf(n)​=Vn​. If Wn​ is finite of size h, then Vn​⊆{0,…,h−1}, so Vn​ is recursive. If Wn​ is infinite, then for every x∈K a sufficiently late stage has both x∈Ks​ and ∣Wn,s​∣>x, while no x∈/K is ever enumerated. Hence Vn​=K, which is not recursive. Therefore n∈P⟺f(n)∈Q,P≤m​Q​. As usual the effective numbering indexes all programs; if malformed codes are included, send them to a fixed index of K.

12B (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 544 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 544
12B OurBigBook.com
A fraction 1−k of adults survives each time step; k is the adult mortality fraction. Adults produce μan​ larvae, which mature one step later with recruitment reduced by adult-dependent competition through 1/(1+an​). Eliminating larvae gives the second-order difference equation
an+1​=(1−k)an​+1+an​μan−1​​.
(22)
At an equilibrium point, either (a,b)=(0,0) or
a∗​=kμ​−1,b∗​=μ(kμ​−1),μ>k.​
(23)
Only nonnegative populations are admissible. At extinction the Jacobian matrix is (1−kμ​10​) and its characteristic polynomial is λ2−(1−k)λ−μ. Its positive root exceeds 1 exactly when μ>k. For 0<μ<k both roots have modulus less than 1; at μ=k the roots are 1,−k, so linearization is marginal. On the nonnegative state space extinction is still attracting at this equality: if two consecutive adult values are bounded by M>0, the next is at most (1−k)M+kM/(1+an​)≤M, with strict decrease away from zero; the maximum of two consecutive adult values strictly decreases after two steps whenever it is positive; continuity on its bounded state region then excludes a positive limiting maximum. Thus the extinction equilibrium point is unstable exactly when the positive equilibrium point exists, with equality understood through nonlinear rather than strict linear stability.
At the positive equilibrium point, the trace and determinant of the Jacobian matrix are T=1−2k+k2/μ and −k. The Jury stability criterion for λ2−Tλ−k requires 1−T−k>0, 1+T−k>0 and 1−k>0. The strict linear stability analysis conditions are
μ>k,(3k−2)μ<k2.​
(24)
For k≤2/3 there is no upper bound on μ; for k>2/3 the stable region is k<μ<k2/(3k−2).
At the lower boundary μ=k, the positive equilibrium point merges with extinction, with a multiplier +1 and slow recovery. At the upper boundary a multiplier reaches −1 (the other is k), giving alternating adult/larval fluctuations. The nonlinear map confirms a supercritical period-doubling bifurcation, as follows. For k>2/3, put h=1−k and μc​=k2/(3k−2). A nonconstant period-two adult sequence A,B satisfies B=hA+μB/(1+A) and A=hB+μA/(1+B). Subtracting and adding these equations gives
S=A+B=hμ−1−h​,P=AB=1+hhS(S+1)​,(A−B)2=1+hS[(1−3h)S−4h]​.
(25)

Zorn lemma states that a partially ordered set in which every chain in a partially ordered set has an upper bound has a maximal element. Include the empty chain in a partially ordered set, so the hypotheses imply that the set P is nonempty. Suppose there were no maximal element. Every chain in a partially ordered set C has an upper bound u, and some v>u; therefore the set of elements strictly above every member of C is nonempty. The axiom of choice selects one such element f(C) for each chain in a partially ordered set (and an element of P when C is empty).
By Hartogs theorem, there is an ordinal κ which does not inject into P. Transfinite recursion defines xα​=f({xβ​:β<α}) for all α<κ: previous elements form a strictly increasing chain in a partially ordered set, including at limit ordinal stages. All xα​ are distinct, giving the forbidden injection. This proves Zorn lemma; the choice of f is the use of the axiom of choice.
Apply Zorn lemma to linearly independent subsets of R over Q, ordered by inclusion. A union along a chain in a partially ordered set is linearly independent because each finite linear relation occurs in one member of that chain in a partially ordered set. A maximal independent set spans R, since a vector outside its span could be adjoined. Thus R has a Hamel basis over Q.
For a finite basis, the Steinitz exchange lemma proves equality of basis sizes. This also rules out an infinite basis when a finite spanning set exists: write each member of the finite spanning set using finitely many elements of another basis; their finite union spans, and independence leaves no other basis elements. If a basis B is infinite with cardinality λ, the finite-support description of every vector and countability of Q give
λ≤∣V∣≤∑n<ω​∣B∣n∣Q∣n=λ.
(33)
Here infinite cardinal arithmetic uses the axiom of choice. Thus any infinite basis has cardinality ∣V∣, proving all bases have the same cardinality. The zero space has its unique empty basis.

A graph Ramsey number R(s,t) is the least N such that every red-blue edge colouring of the complete graph KN​ has a red Ks​ or a blue Kt​. At a vertex in KR(s−1,t)+R(s,t−1)​, either at least R(s−1,t) neighbours have red incident edges or at least R(s,t−1) have blue incident edges. In the first case find a red Ks−1​ and adjoin the vertex, or a blue Kt​; the second case is symmetric. Thus
R(s,t)≤R(s−1,t)+R(s,t−1).
(34)
Starting with R(2,t)=t and R(s,2)=s, induction gives the binomial upper bound for a Ramsey number
R(s,t)≤(s−1s+t−2​),R(s,s)≤(s−12s−2​)≤4s−1<4s.​
(35)
For the lower construction, partition 2t−2 vertices into two classes of size t−1, colour inside-class edges red and between-class edges blue. Red cliques have at most t−1 vertices, and the blue graph is bipartite, so has no odd cycle.
Conversely, a graph without an odd cycle is bipartite: in each connected component colour vertices by the parity of the length of a path from a root; differing path parities would give an odd closed walk, hence an odd cycle. On 2t−1 vertices one of the two blue bipartition classes has at least t vertices. Every edge within it is red, giving a red Kt​. Thus 2t−1 is the exact threshold for this alternative.

Burnside's theorem states that every finite group of order paqb is solvable, where p,q are primes and a,b are nonnegative integers. In particular, a nonabelian simple group cannot have order divisible by only one or two distinct primes.

Conjugation by P partitions H into orbits. Each non-singleton orbit has size divisible by p, by the orbit-stabilizer theorem. The singleton orbits are exactly H∩Z(P). Since ∣H∣ is divisible by p, ∣H∩Z(P)∣≡0(modp). This set contains 1, so ∣H∩Z(P)∣≥p​.
For the deduction we also give the representation-theoretic ingredient behind Burnside's theorem: a nonabelian finite simple group has no nontrivial conjugacy class of prime power size. Here is a proof, so no stronger theorem is being assumed without justification. Suppose g=1 has class size pb. For an irreducible character χ of degree d coprime to p, the class sum acts as the scalar pbχ(g)/d, which is an algebraic integer: the class sum has an integer-entry matrix in the regular representation, which contains every irreducible representation, so this scalar is an eigenvalue of an integer-entry matrix. Also χ(g) is an algebraic integer. Bezout's identity then makes χ(g)/d an algebraic integer. All its algebraic conjugates have modulus at most 1, because character values of a representation are sums of d roots of unity. An algebraic integer with this property is zero or a root of unity: the monic polynomials of all its powers have uniformly bounded integer coefficients, so two powers must coincide unless it is zero.
Every nontrivial irreducible representation of a simple group is faithful. If χ(g)/d were a root of unity, equality in the triangle inequality would force its representing matrix to be scalar, hence g central, impossible. Thus χ(g)=0 whenever p∤d, except for the trivial character of a representation. Orthogonality of the identity column and the g column in the character table now gives
0=1+∑p∣χ(1)​χ(1)χ(g)​.
(38)
This would make 1/p an algebraic integer, contradicting the fact that rational algebraic integers are integers. The same proof covers class size 1 directly through triviality of the center.
If an abelian subgroup A had index pa, every g∈A∖{1} would have A⊆CG​(g), making its class size a divisor of pa, a contradiction. Such a g exists: if A=1, then G is a nontrivial p-group, whose center is nontrivial by the first argument with H=P. Therefore a nonabelian simple group has no abelian subgroup of prime power index.

By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, every competitor has E≥L2/(2(b−a)), with equality for constant speed, so this parametrization also minimizes E. For a fixed-endpoint variation with tangential vector field V, differentiation and integration by parts give

The original parameter need not be affine: arbitrary varying-speed parametrizations preserve length but have nonzero covariant acceleration. This qualification is necessary for the literal wording.
For distinct nonantipodal p,q on the punctured unit sphere, there is a unique shorter great circle arc, of length d=arccos(p⋅q)<π. A minimizing curve exists exactly when that shorter arc avoids the removed north pole. If it avoids the pole it attains the spherical lower bound. If it passes through the pole, arbitrarily small smooth detours have lengths tending to d, but equality would force the unique shorter arc, which is unavailable. Thus the infimum is not attained; the longer great circle arc is not a substitute minimizer.
For antipodal p,q in the punctured sphere, one can choose a great circle semicircle avoiding the north pole; it attains length π. Thus every admissible antipodal pair has a minimizer. If identical endpoints are included despite the earlier distinctness stipulation, the infimum is zero, but no smooth regular curve attains it; only a nonregular constant curve does.

In a neutral Moran model, a population has N labelled individuals; reproduction copies one individual's type to a uniformly chosen other individual, keeping population size fixed. One convenient time convention puts independent rate-1/2 Poisson arrows on each ordered pair of distinct individuals. Backwards in time, two sampled ancestral lineages merge whenever one copies the other, at total rate 1 per unordered pair. In the convention where each individual reproduces at rate 1, this pair rate is 2/(N−1) if the parent cannot replace itself, and time must be rescaled accordingly.
Kingman's coalescent on n labels is the continuous-time Markov chain on partitions of {1,…,n}, initially all singleton blocks, in which each pair of distinct blocks merges at rate 1. With j blocks, the waiting time is exponential of rate (2j​), and the merging pair is uniform. Kingman's infinite coalescent is the consistent partition process on N whose restriction to each finite label set has this law; consistency and the extension theorem construct it. These time conventions are part of the definition.
Let Bt(n)​ be the number of blocks in the first n labels. The expected time to reach at most m blocks is
ETm(n)​=∑j=m+1n​(2j​)−1=2(m1​−n1​)≤m2​.
(53)
Markov inequality gives P(Bt(n)​>m)≤2/(mt). As n increases these counts increase to the total number of infinite-coalescent blocks, so the same bound holds for that number. Letting m→∞ shows it is finite almost surely for each t>0. Apply this simultaneously to positive rational times; monotonicity of the block count then covers every positive real time. Hence Kingman's infinite coalescent comes down from infinity almost surely.

A renewal process has independent identically distributed, nonnegative, almost surely finite inter-arrival times Xi​, epochs S0​=0,Sn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, and count N(t)=max{n:Sn​≤t}. Allowing zero inter-arrivals is harmless provided P(X1​>0)>0. The hypothesis EX1​>0 ensures there is ε>0 with p=P(X1​≥ε)>0.
The strong law of large numbers for the indicators gives Sn​≥ε∑i=1n​1Xi​≥ε​→∞, so N(t) is finite for finite t. Conversely every fixed Sn​ is finite, so eventually N(t)≥n. On their countable common probability-one event, this proves N(t)→∞ as t→∞ almost surely​.
For fixed t, put L=⌊t/ε⌋. The hinted comparison process has epochs Sn′​=ε∑i=1n​1Xi​≥ε​≤Sn​, hence N(t)≤N′(t). Equivalently,
P(N(t)≥n)≤P(Bin(n,p)≤L).
(54)
If p<1, for n>L this is bounded by Ct,p​nL(1−p)n, by summing the first L+1 binomial distribution. Thus ∑n​eθnP(N(t)=n)<∞ for 0<θ<−log(1−p). If p=1, N(t)≤L deterministically. Therefore a strictly positive exponential moment exists for every fixed finite t, with the same allowed θ for all such t. Almost-sure finiteness of the inter-arrivals is implicit in a proper renewal process; allowing an infinite inter-arrival with positive probability would invalidate the divergence claim.

The centre manifold theorem gives, near an equilibrium of a sufficiently smooth system, a local invariant manifold tangent to the generalized eigenspaces with zero-real-part eigenvalues, expressible as a graph of a function over them. Its reduced dynamics govern local equilibria and their stability in the presence of strictly stable transverse directions. The manifold need not be unique or analytic; finite Taylor jets can nevertheless be determined from invariance. Treating a parameter as a variable with μ˙​=0 gives the extended centre manifold for a parameter.
At r=1 the linearized (x,y) block has eigenvalues 0,−2, and the z direction has eigenvalue −1. Thus the origin is a nonhyperbolic equilibrium, with stable dimension two and non-extended centre dimension one. The extended centre dimension is two. The transformed equations are
u˙v˙z˙​=21​μ(u+v)+2a​(u+v)3−21​(u−v)z,=−2v−21​μ(u+v)+2a​(u+v)3+21​(u−v)z,=u2−v2−z,μ˙​=0.​

Here Ow​(j) means terms of weighted order at least j under the stated scaling. If a<1, the pitchfork bifurcation is supercritical: stable branches u∼±μ/(1−a)​ appear for μ>0 as the origin loses stability. If a>1, it is a subcritical pitchfork bifurcation: unstable branches occur for μ<0, while the origin is stable there.
For a=1, assign μ weight four. The leading cubic terms in u˙ cancel. The invariance equations now give V=u3/2+Ow​(5) and Z=u2+0u4+Ow​(6): Zu​u˙ first contributes at weight six and v2 also first contributes there. Substitution then gives

The derivative along the nonzero branches is −2μ>0, so they are unstable. The origin is stable for μ<0, unstable for μ>0, and nonlinearly unstable at μ=0 because the leading term is +u5. This is a degenerate subcritical pitchfork bifurcation.

A clockwise engine Carnot cycle has four reversible steps. At hot temperature Th​, isothermal expansion absorbs Qh​=Th​ΔS>0 and does positive work by the gas. Adiabatic expansion then cools it to Tc​, with zero heat and positive work by the gas. Isothermal compression at Tc​ emits Qc​=−Tc​ΔS and requires work on the gas. Finally adiabatic compression returns it to Th​, with zero heat and work on the gas.
For an ideal gas, the p,V isotherms obey pV=constant and the adiabats pVγ=constant, the latter being steeper. In the T,S plane, the isotherms are horizontal and the adiabats vertical, forming a clockwise rectangle. Heat occurs only on the horizontal legs, while work occurs on all four p,V legs.

For the two infinite sheets, superposition and the electromagnetic field jumps give E=(σ/ϵ0​)ex​, B=μ0​Key​ between them and zero outside. Substitution yields exactly
σij​=2ϵ0​σ2​diag(−1,1,1)+2μ0​K2​diag(1,−1,1).
(92)
A thin pillbox enclosing the x=0 sheet has only its +x face in the interior electromagnetic field. Therefore
AF​=(2ϵ0​σ2​−2μ0​K2​)ex​.​
(93)
Directly, omit the sheet's self-electromagnetic field: the other sheet supplies Eother​=σex​/(2ϵ0​) and Bother​=μ0​Key​/2. The Lorentz force per area is σEother​+Kez​×Bother​, giving the same result. The electric contribution is attractive and the magnetic contribution repulsive.
If K=σv for a single moving charge population, use μ0​ϵ0​=c−2 to obtain F/A=σ2(1−v2/c2)ex​/(2ϵ0​). For physical ∣v∣<c this is attractive, so motion of these charges cannot make the force repulsive. Independently imposed currents need not satisfy that restriction on K/σ.

Solution

Words: 50
i OurBigBook.com
At p, choose local normal coordinates with gαβ​(p)=diag(−1,1). Let e0​,e1​ be their coordinate basis. The vectors V=e0​+e1​ and W=e0​−e1​ have zero metric tensor square, and their component matrix has determinant −2=0. Thus two independent null vectors form a basis of the tangent space. Normal coordinates are only needed at the chosen point, not on a whole neighbourhood with flat metric.

ii

Words: 40 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 40
ii OurBigBook.com
Write the nonzero tangent vector as U=aV+bW. Since g(V,V)=g(W,W)=0 and g(V,W)=−2, nullness gives g(U,U)=−4ab=0. Thus exactly one coefficient can be nonzero, proving U∥V or U∥W​. This pointwise argument does not require the curve to be a geodesic.

iii

Words: 96 Articles: 1
36D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 96
iii OurBigBook.com
Let U be the smooth nonzero tangent along a regular null curve, and a=∇U​U. Metric compatibility gives g(U,a)=21​U[g(U,U)]=0. In a two-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, the orthogonal complement of a nonzero null vector is its own span; this follows directly in the preceding null basis. Therefore a=κ(t)U.
Consequently every regular null curve is a geodesic up to reparametrization. To obtain an affine parameter λ, write q=dt/dλ>0 and solve dq/dt+κ(t)q=0. Then ∇qU​(qU)=q2(κ+q−1dq/dt)U=0. A solution q=Cexp(−∫κdt) exists locally and along any nonsingular parameter interval. The original parameter need not be affine; the literal assertion of zero covariant acceleration for every parameter would be false.

iv

Solution

Words: 51
iv OurBigBook.com
In Minkowski spacetime with metric −dt2+dx2+dy2+dz2, take
γ(t)=(t,cost,sint,0).​
(94)
Its tangent vector is (1,−sint,cost,0), with metric tensor square −1+sin2t+cos2t=0. Its acceleration is (0,−cost,−sint,0), nonzero and not proportional to the tangent because its time component is zero. Thus it is a regular null curve which is not a geodesic under any reparametrization.

Words: 149
37B OurBigBook.com
Write Q=Uj​xj​ and use repeated-index summation. Direct differentiation gives
∂j​ui​=2a​[−r3Ui​xj​​+r3Uj​xi​​+r3Qδij​​−r53Qxi​xj​​].
(95)
Tracing yields ∂i​ui​=0. Since ∇2(1/r)=0 for r>a, and ∇2(Qxi​/r3)=2Ui​/r3−6Qxi​/r5, we get
μ∇2ui​=μa(r3Ui​​−r53Qxi​​)=∂i​p.
(96)
Hence the incompressible Stokes equations hold everywhere outside the bubble.
The Newtonian viscous stress tensor Tij​=−pδij​+μ(∂j​ui​+∂i​uj​) simplifies to
Tij​=−r53μaQxi​xj​​.​
(97)
At r=a with n=x/a, u=21​[U+(U⋅n)n], so u⋅n=U⋅n: the interface is impermeable in the bubble frame. Also Tn=−(3μ/a)(U⋅n)n is purely normal, so the tangential traction vanishes, appropriate to a clean bubble with negligible internal viscosity. The tangential fluid velocity need not equal the bubble's velocity. At infinity u,p→0. The calculation assumes the usual spherical, negligible-deformation limit; exact normal-stress balance includes interior pressure, surface tension and any buoyancy sustaining the motion.
Integrate the outer-fluid traction with the normal pointing from the bubble into the fluid:
Fi​=−a3μ​Uj​∫ni​nj​dS=−4πμaUi​.
(98)
Thus Fdrag​=−4πμaU​, smaller than the no-slip rigid-sphere Stokes drag law −6πμaU.

38B (Waves)

Words: 244 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 244
38B OurBigBook.com
For the rapidly varying wave phase, define ki​=∂i​θ and ω=−∂t​θ, with the common scaling by ε absorbed into these local variables. A packet moves with group velocity cg,i​=∂Ω/∂ki​. Along that trajectory, d/dt=∂t​+cg​⋅∇x​. Compatibility gives ∂t​ki​=−∂i​ω and ∂i​kj​=∂j​ki​. Differentiating the local dispersion relation then cancels its implicit k derivatives, yielding
x˙i​=Ωki​​,k˙i​=−Ωxi​​,ω˙=Ωt​.​
(99)
The last equality follows also by differentiating ω=Ω(k,x,t) along the ray and cancelling the two Hamiltonian cross terms. The partial derivatives of Ω hold its other arguments fixed.
A mean flow adds the Doppler shift: the intrinsic frequency is ω=ω−kU(z), so
(ω−kU)2=k2+m2N2k2​,Ω=kU+k2+m2​Nk​
(100)
on the positive-intrinsic-frequency branch launched here. The medium is stationary and independent of x, so ω and k are constant. Initially m=0,U=0, hence ω=N. Moreover m˙=−kU′<0, and then z˙=−Nkm/(k2+m2)3/2>0. The initial vertical group velocity is zero, but m immediately becomes negative and the ray accelerates upwards.
If U reaches N/k at a finite height zc​, this is the critical level of an internal gravity wave, with U(zc​)=ω/k. Below it,
m=−k(N−kU)2N2​−1​.​
(101)
Assuming 0<U′(zc​)<∞, put δ=zc​−z. Then N−kU∼kU′(zc​)δ, giving
m∼−U′(zc​)δN​,z˙∼NkU′(zc​)2​δ2,t∼kU′(zc​)2δN​⟶∞.​
(102)
Thus the ray cannot cross this level in finite time within the geometrical-optics approximation. The hypothesis U′>0,U(0)=0 alone does not guarantee a finite zc​: for example U(z)=2kN​(1−e−z) on z≥0 never reaches N/k. Existence of a finite critical level is an additional assumption. Very close to one, diverging wavenumber can invalidate the inviscid, linear, slowly varying approximation; the result is the formal ray prediction.

i OurBigBook.com
Expand the initial vector in the orthonormal eigenbasis. After j unshifted steps, the coefficient ratio of mode i<n to the dominant mode is (ci​/cn​)(λi​/λn​)j. Since λn−1​=1 and cn−1​,cn​=0, the sharp asymptotic contraction factor is
ρ=1+ϵ1​=1−ϵ+O(ϵ2).​
(103)
Normalization only changes the dominant coefficient by a higher-order error; its eventual sign is the sign of cn​.

ii

Words: 42 Articles: 1
39A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 42
ii OurBigBook.com
With shift 1/2, the unwanted eigenvalues lie in [−1/2,1/2], and both endpoints occur. The dominant shifted eigenvalue is 1/2+ϵ. Hence
ρ=1/2+ϵ1/2​=1−2ϵ+O(ϵ2).​
(104)
The negative endpoint can alternate in sign, but the norm error has this factor, and the even-iteration comparison removes the alternation.

iii

Words: 109 Articles: 1
39A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 109
iii OurBigBook.com
Two consecutive steps multiply by the polynomial of the symmetric matrix
P(A)=(A−s0​I)(A−s1​I),P(λ)=λ2−λ+81​=81​T2​(2λ−1).
(105)
The Chebyshev polynomial bound on [0,1] gives ∣P(λ)∣≤1/8, and the actual endpoints 0,1 attain it. At the dominant eigenvalue, P(1+ϵ)=1/8+ϵ+ϵ2. Thus
ρ2=1+8ϵ+8ϵ21​,ρ=1−4ϵ+O(ϵ2).​
(106)
For a small prescribed error δ relative to a fixed initial-component factor C, the number of matrix-vector iterations is approximately log(C/δ)/(−logρ). The three leading denominators are ϵ,2ϵ,4ϵ. Therefore the iteration counts are in the ratio 1:1/2:1/4: the single shift halves and the alternating double shift quarters the leading count. A pair of double-shift steps costs two matrix-vector products, already accounted for by using ρ per iteration rather than ρ2.
